aliases.note: Sugar on its own usually means sucrose, table sugar.
aliases.hint: Sugar on its own usually means sucrose, table sugar. There are several different sugars (glucose, fructose, lactose, maltose and more), and each is a different molecule.

aliases.note: Table sugar is sucrose: one glucose unit joined to one fructose unit.
Brown sugar is mostly sucrose with a little molasses left in it.
Blood sugar is glucose. Dissolved glucose is a mixture of ring forms; the alpha and beta rings are the two here.
Fruit sugar is fructose.
Milk sugar is lactose: one glucose unit joined to one galactose unit.
Malt sugar is maltose: two glucose units joined.
Sweetness is how the tongue reports sugars such as these. Artificial sweeteners are different molecules that are not in the explorer.
Honey is mostly the sugars fructose and glucose with a little water; bees make it from nectar, which is mostly sucrose.
Starch is a long chain of glucose units; plants store energy in it.
Cellulose is a long chain of glucose units that plants build their cell walls from.
Cotton and paper are mostly cellulose; the model is a short piece of a cellulose chain.
Wood is mostly cellulose and lignin.

aliases.hint: Several different sugars share the formula C6H12O6: glucose, fructose and galactose are all built from the same atoms in different arrangements.
Several different sugars share the formula C12H22O11: sucrose, lactose and maltose are the common ones.
Two different molecules share the formula C4H10: butane and isobutane.

aliases.note: Table salt is sodium chloride. In the solid, sodium and chloride ions sit in a cubic lattice; halite is the mineral.
aliases.hint: Salt in the kitchen is sodium chloride (NaCl). In chemistry, "a salt" can mean any compound made of ions.

aliases.note: Sea salt is mostly sodium chloride.
Baking soda is sodium hydrogencarbonate (NaHCO3). The explorer has its bicarbonate ion (HCO3-), the part that does the chemistry, but not the solid.
Washing soda is sodium carbonate (Na2CO3). The explorer has the carbonate ion, not the solid.
Vinegar is mostly water with a few per cent acetic acid, which is what makes it sour and sharp.
Lemon juice is sour mainly from citric acid (the model is citrate, its ion). Limonene is the oil in citrus peel that smells of lemon and orange.
Yeast ferments sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide; the gas makes bread rise.
Milk contains the sugar lactose and fats; this is a card about each, not a model of milk.
The bubbles in fizzy drinks are carbon dioxide gas dissolved under pressure.
Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide.
Capsaicin is the molecule that makes chilli peppers burn.
Menthol gives mint its cool feeling.
Vanillin is the main flavour molecule of vanilla.
Curcumin is the yellow-orange pigment of turmeric.
Beta-carotene is the orange pigment in carrots; the body can turn it into vitamin A.
Lycopene is the red pigment in tomatoes.
Blue jeans are dyed with indigo.
Cyanidin is one of the anthocyanin pigments that colour many red, purple and blue fruits and flowers.
Chlorophyll a is the main green pigment that catches light for photosynthesis.
Coffee, tea and many cola drinks contain caffeine; coffee itself is a mixture of hundreds of compounds.
Chocolate contains a little caffeine.
The alcohol in drinks is ethanol.
Rubbing alcohol is usually isopropanol (isopropyl alcohol); many hand sanitisers use ethanol or isopropanol.
Car antifreeze is mostly ethylene glycol.
Nail polish remover is usually acetone.
Petrol is a mixture of many hydrocarbons; octane (C8H18) is one of them.
Camping gas and lighter fuel are mostly propane or butane.
Natural gas is mostly methane.
Fire is a fast reaction of a fuel with oxygen that gives out heat and light. Burning methane makes carbon dioxide and water.
TNT is a well-known explosive.
Traditional mothballs are naphthalene.
Laughing gas is nitrous oxide.
Hydrogen sulfide smells of rotten eggs.
Car (lead-acid) batteries contain sulfuric acid.
Stomach acid is mostly hydrochloric acid, which is hydrogen chloride dissolved in water.
Acid rain comes mainly from sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides that turn into sulfuric and nitric acids.
Fertilisers supply nitrogen (as ammonium or nitrate) and phosphorus (as phosphate).
Chlorine gas is the element Cl2; household bleach is a different compound (sodium hypochlorite) that the explorer does not have.
Freon is a brand name for CFC refrigerants; CFC-12 is one of them.
Carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide are greenhouse gases.
Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas from incomplete burning.
Helium is the light gas used in balloons.
Water is H2O: one oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms.
Ordinary ice is the crystal Ice Ih. Snowflakes are ice crystals.
Steam is water as a gas; each molecule is the same H2O.
Urea is the main nitrogen-containing waste in urine.
Too much uric acid in the blood can form crystals in joints and cause gout.
Soaps are salts of fatty acids: a long oily tail and a charged head. Stearic acid is the acid form of a common soap ingredient.
Fats and oils are triglycerides: three fatty acids on a glycerol backbone. Tripalmitin is one example.
Oleic acid is the main fatty acid in olive oil.
Proteins are long chains of amino acids. The model is a short five-glycine chain.
There are 20 standard amino acids; the explorer has models of all of them.

aliases.hint: There are many vitamins; these are the ones with models.

aliases.note: Vitamin C is ascorbic acid.
Vitamin A is retinol (and related molecules such as retinal).
Vitamin D3 is cholecalciferol; skin makes it in sunlight.
ATP is the molecule cells use to pay for work.
Common painkillers: paracetamol (acetaminophen), ibuprofen and aspirin act differently.
Advil and Nurofen are brand names of ibuprofen.
Paracetamol and acetaminophen are the same molecule; Tylenol and Panadol are brand names.
Morphine is the main active alkaloid of opium.
THC is the main psychoactive molecule of cannabis.
Nicotine is the addictive molecule in tobacco.
Valium is a brand name of diazepam.
Lidocaine is a common local anaesthetic.
Cisplatin is one chemotherapy drug.
L-DOPA is used to treat Parkinson's disease; the brain turns it into dopamine.
Adrenaline and epinephrine are the same molecule.
Cortisol is often called the stress hormone.
Serotonin and dopamine are chemical messengers involved in mood and reward; "happy hormone" is a simplification.
Estradiol is the main oestrogen.
Insulin is a protein, which the explorer does not model; the cards cover how blood sugar is controlled.
Roundup's active ingredient is glyphosate.
DNA has four bases: adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine; RNA uses uracil in place of thymine.

aliases.hint: There are many plastics. These models are short pieces of the most common long chains.

aliases.note: Carrier bags and milk bottles are polyethylene (polythene).
Drinks bottles and polyester fibre are PET.
Styrofoam is a brand name for polystyrene foam.
Teflon is the brand name of PTFE.
Nylon 6,6 is one common nylon.
Kevlar is an aramid fibre.
Natural rubber is polyisoprene.
Silk, wool and hair are made of proteins; the explorer has the general protein card and a short peptide, not these fibres.
Common glass is mostly silicon dioxide but has no crystal structure; quartz is crystalline silicon dioxide, the nearest thing here.
There is no model of a ceramic yet. Many ceramics are made from clay and silica, so quartz and the silicate molecules are related materials.
Sand is mostly grains of quartz, which is silicon dioxide.
Clays are layered silicates; these are building blocks of silicate minerals.
Limestone, chalk and marble are mostly calcium carbonate, the mineral calcite; eggshell and seashell are mostly calcium carbonate too.
Cement is made by heating limestone (calcium carbonate) with clay. Concrete itself is a composite, not a single crystal.
Granite is made of mineral grains such as quartz.

aliases.hint: A crystal is a solid whose atoms sit in a repeating pattern. These are some you can fly into.

aliases.note: Olivine is a mineral series; forsterite is its magnesium end member.
Fool's gold is pyrite, iron sulfide.
Titanium dioxide, mineral form rutile, is the white pigment in most paint and a UV blocker in many sunscreens.
Diamond is a crystal of pure carbon.
Pencil "lead" is graphite mixed with clay; there is no lead in it.
Coal and charcoal are mostly carbon but not crystalline; diamond and graphite are the two crystalline forms.
Steel is iron with a little carbon (and other metals in stainless steel); iron is the crystal here.
Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide. The nearest crystal the explorer has is hematite, iron(III) oxide (Fe2O3); rust itself is a looser mix that holds water, so this is a close relative, not rust.
Magnetite is a naturally magnetic mineral (lodestone). Everyday magnets are made of other materials.
Electrical wire is usually copper (or aluminium).
Foil and drinks cans are aluminium.
Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.
Bronze is an alloy of copper, usually with tin.
Chips are cut from wafers of nearly perfect silicon crystal.

aliases.hint: Metals are crystals of atoms that share their outer electrons. These are four you can fly into.

aliases.note: Lithium is the element behind lithium-ion batteries.
Potassium is the element K; bananas are known for containing it.
Na comes from the Latin natrium.
K comes from the Latin kalium.
Fe comes from the Latin ferrum.
Au comes from the Latin aurum.
Ag comes from the Latin argentum.
Pb comes from the Latin plumbum.
Sn comes from the Latin stannum.
Cu comes from the Latin cuprum.
Hg comes from the Greek-Latin hydrargyrum.
W comes from wolfram, the old name of tungsten.
In the body view choose Skeleton at the top to see every bone.
The tailbone (coccyx) sits just below the sacrum; the model shows the sacrum.
Lactate builds up in muscles during hard exercise.
The heartbeat starts in a small patch of cells called the sinoatrial node.
The heart's natural pacemaker is the sinoatrial node.
There is no 3D model of blood itself; the blood vessels it flows in are here, and the cards describe its cells.
Haemoglobin carries oxygen on an iron atom held in a heme group.
Stool forms in the large intestine, mostly from undigested food, bacteria and water.
The pupil is the opening in the iris.
The retina has three kinds of cone cells; colour blindness is usually a missing or altered kind.
The human ear has no 3D model yet; the dog's ear (eardrum, cochlea) is modelled and works the same way.
Hair grows from a follicle in the skin; hair itself is mostly the protein keratin.
Melanocytes make melanin, the pigment that darkens skin.
There is no 3D virus model yet; the cards explain how viruses are built and how they replicate.
There is no 3D bacterium model yet; the cards describe bacterial cells.
There is no model of a hen's egg yet; the cards describe the egg cell, the cell that starts a new life.

aliases.hint: Nucleus can mean the centre of a cell or the centre of an atom.

aliases.note: Mitochondria make most of a cell's ATP.
Birds are living dinosaurs; there is no dinosaur model yet.
The dog is a full anatomical model in the park: coat, skeleton, muscles, organs.
Bees are a full model in the park; other insects are described on the insects card.

aliases.note: The flower in the park is a meadow buttercup.
No fish or frog model yet; this card covers them.
No cat, horse or whale model yet. The mammals card covers them, and the dog is a full mammal model.
There is no model of these insects yet; the honeybee is a full insect model.
The phone in your hand opens into its parts, and the battery is one of them: a lithium-ion cell. There is no model of a battery cell cut open yet.

q: how electricity gets to my house

aliases.note: Static electricity is charge that has built up on a surface, as in lightning.
Lightning is a huge spark of static electricity inside a storm cloud.
Solar cells are usually made of silicon; the explorer has cards and a lab but no model of a solar panel yet.
The smallest motor in the explorer is the vibration motor inside the phone; the cards cover larger motors.
The phone in your hand opens into its parts.
The phone's motion sensors are modelled; its microphone is not.
Wi-Fi sends data as radio waves, mainly in the 2.4 and 5 GHz bands.
GPS satellites need corrections from relativity to stay accurate.
A modern chip holds billions of transistors; each is a tiny switch.
An LED makes light when electrons cross a band gap in a semiconductor.
Old filament bulbs glow because a hot wire gives out thermal radiation; LEDs work differently.
Microwave ovens use radio waves that are absorbed by water in food.
A compass needle lines up with Earth's magnetic field.
The sky is blue because air scatters blue light more strongly than red light.
Near sunrise and sunset sunlight crosses far more air, which scatters the blue away and leaves red and orange.
A rainbow is sunlight bent and reflected inside raindrops, which spreads it into its colours.
Dry air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen.
Tides are mainly raised by the Moon's gravity.
Oil is a mixture of many hydrocarbon molecules.

aliases.note: The Sun is a star: a ball of hot plasma held together by its own gravity.
Mars is red because of iron oxide in its dust.
Ceres is the largest body in the asteroid belt (it is also a dwarf planet).

aliases.note: Every atom has a tiny nucleus surrounded by a cloud of electrons.
A proton is made of three quarks: two up and one down.
The explorer opens in a park. Scroll to zoom, click anything for a card, and use the ruler on the left to fly to other scales. Choose Help (top right) for the full guide.
There is no model of this vitamin yet; the card covers cofactors, coenzymes and vitamins.
Graphene is a single layer of the carbon sheets that stack to make graphite.
Carbon fibre is made of thin threads of carbon in graphite-like layers.
Diamond and quartz (which includes amethyst) are gem minerals. Ruby and emerald are other minerals the explorer does not have yet.
A light-year is the distance light travels in a year, about 9.46 trillion kilometres.
Relativity says clocks can run at different rates; the cards cover what physics says about time.
The phone's battery is one lithium-ion pouch cell: it opens into its layers.
In a lithium-ion cell the negative electrode is graphite on copper foil.
In a phone cell the positive electrode is lithium cobalt oxide on aluminium foil.
Lithium sits between the carbon sheets of graphite: LiC6 when full.
No model of a solid-state cell exists; the card says what is known and what is not.
